{{Lunisolar December}} {{Lunisolar June}} {{Short description|Japanese purification rite and festival}} {{Expand Japanese|大祓|date=November 2023}} {{Use dmy dates|date=December 2023}} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} The {{Nihongo|2=大祓式|3='''Ōharae-shiki'''}} is one of the [[Shinto]] purification rituals known as ''[[harae]]'' and is sometimes translated as "Great Purification".{{Cite web |last=Namiki |first=Kazuko |title=Ōharae |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9119 |access-date=9 November 2023 |website=[[Kokugakuin University]] Encyclopedia of Shinto}} It is also known as the {{Nihongo|2=中臣の祓|3=Nakatomi no harae}}. The ''[[Oharae no Kotoba|Ōharae no Kotoba]]'' prayer is recited during the ritual. The ritual is performed biannually on June 30{{Cite web |title=Nagoshi no Oharae Purification Ritual |url=https://www.kamigamojinja.jp/en/rituals/nagoshi-no-oharae-purification-ritual/ |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Kamo Wakeikazuchi Jinja Shrine (Kamigamo Jinja) |language=ja}} and December 30{{Cite web |last=Meador |first=Spencer |date=2017-07-04 |title=Oharae |url=http://sanpai-japan.com/2017/07/04/oharae/ |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Sanpai Japan |language=en-US}} at several shrines, but also as necessary, such as after an offense is committed, at the [[Daijosai]], or when an unmarried prince or princess departs the imperial palace to visit [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]] or the [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrines]].{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016-11-11 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-062171-1 |edition=Illustrated |location=New York (N.Y.) |language=English}}{{rp|7}} The December 30 ritual is sometimes held on New Year's Eve.{{Cite web |title=Shiwasu Oharae-shiki (Great Purification Ceremony in December) {{!}} Samukawa-jinja Shrine |url=https://samukawajinjya.jp/en/festival/shiwasuoharae.html |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Samukawa-jinja Shrine Official Website |language=en}} == History == The primary theory is that the ''Ōharae-shiki'' began at the end of the seventh century. It evolved over time, especially through the fifteenth century. These changes were linked to modifications to the [[Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]], a set of laws and rules, in the eighth century. The ''Ōharae-shiki'' changed again in the [[Edo period]] (1603–1868), and some previous aspects were reestablished during the [[Meiji era|Meiji period]] (1868–1912). Purification became more important to prepare for this ritual and {{ill|Yoori|ja|節折|1=Yoori|2=ja|3=節折|4=fr|5=Yoori|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=}} became more prominent in the Meiji restoration.{{rp|362}}{{Clarify|date=January 2025|reason=This ritual is already for purification. Did other purification became more important? What is Yoori?}} == ''Minazuki-barae'' == Though the ''Ōharae-shiki'' conducted in June is sometimes confused with the {{Nihongo|2=水無月祓|3=Minazuki-barae}}—another purification rite that takes place at that time in the imperial court—they are conducted separately. ==Notelist== {{Notelist}} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Authority control}} {{citation needed}} {{citation needed}} {{Japanese Lunisolar Calendar}} ==Overview== {{Infobox Holiday | holiday_name = '''Ōharae''' (大祓) | type = Asian holiday | longtype = [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] rite | image = Ooharae-chinowa,katori-jingu,katori-city,japan.JPG | caption = A {{ill|Chinowa|de|Chinowa|ja|茅の輪|zh|茅之輪|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chinowa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓}} ring set up on the approach at [[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Shrine]] | official_name = Ōharae | nickname = Nagoshi-no-Harae, Natsu-Harae, Nagoshi, Minazuki-Harae | date = 30 June (Gregorian)
30 Sixth Month (lunisolar) | celebrations = Passing through the ''chinowa'', use of ''hitogata'' paper figures | relatedto = {{ill|Toshikoshi no Harae|de|Toshikoshi no Harae|ja|年越の祓|zh|年越之祓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toshikoshi no Harae|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} }} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} '''Ōharae''' (おおはらえ・おおはらい) is one of the major rites of [[:en:Harae|Harae]] in the [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] tradition of [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Grounded in the traditional Japanese concern for ritual purity, it aims to cleanse the mind and body of defilements (''kegare'') and remove the various sins and errors that give rise to misfortune, so that people may live each day with a pure and tranquil heart.{{Cite book|language=ja|title=神道いろは―神社とまつりの基礎知識―|date=2007-01-25|publisher=神社新報社|page=116|editor={{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|de|Jinja-honchō|ja|神社本庁教学研究所|zh|神社本庁教学研究所|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Association of Shinto Shrines|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}}} While purification rites (''harae'') are performed routinely at the {{ill|Imperial Court|de|Japanischer Kaiserhof|ja|宮中|zh|日本皇宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Court|qq=}} and in [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]], the twice-yearly ceremonies held for the benefit of all under heaven are distinguished by the name '''Ō-harae''' (“great purification”).''Sekai Daihyakka-jiten'' 2nd ed., s.v. "Ōharae". By long custom the rite is observed on the last day of the Sixth and Twelfth Months—that is, 30 June and 31 December in the modern calendar. In former times it was also conducted ad hoc, for example before and after the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]] (the first ''Niiname-sai'' after an [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor of Japan]]’s accession), in response to unprecedented epidemics or disasters, or to purify candidates for the offices of [[:en:Saikū|Saigū]] and [[:en:Saiin (priestess)|Saiin]]. The ceremony is also called the "Purification of the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]]" ('''Nakatomi-no-Harae'''). == Overview == The earliest textual attestation appears in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], in the section on [[:en:Emperor Chūai|Emperor Chūai]]: {{quote|Take also the great offerings (''Ō-nusa'') of the land and perform a '''great purification''', removing the sins of raw-hide flaying, reverse flaying, dam-filling, dung-gate, incest, bestiality with horse, ox, fowl, and dog…|Adapted from the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], Chūai no Maki}} These offences are collectively known as [[:en:Tsumi|Heavenly sins and earthly sins]]. Because ordinary sins (''tsumi'') and ritual defilements (''kegare'') could not be removed by the short everyday formulas (''harae-kotoba''), the lengthy '''Ō-harae Norito''' was proclaimed to cleanse them. The prayer lists the heavenly sins, which largely concern violations of agricultural taboos, before the earthly sins, implying that in ancient times the former were seen as the graver threat to communal order. Originally the texts for the Sixth- and Twelfth-Month rites differed, but the [[:en:Engishiki|Engishiki]] notes "The Twelfth-Month rite shall follow the precedent of the Sixth," so only the Sixth-Month version survives. While today the norito is recited to the kami, the version in the ''Engishiki'' makes clear that the officiant first calls upon the assembled participants to listen, they respond "Ō" (''isshō''), and only then follows the mythic preamble, enumeration of sins, and description of how the {{ill|Haraedo no Kami|de|Haraedo-no-kami|ja|祓戸大神|zh|祓戶大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haraedo no Kami|qq=}} carry them away. Thus Ō-harae not only "resets" calamities that have already occurred and prays for the tranquillity of the realm, it also functioned as a public proclamation of the taboos imposed by the ruling authority.''Sekai Daihyakka-jiten'', 2nd ed., s.v. "Kodai-hō" (ancient law). In 1914 (Taishō 3) the Ministry of Home Affairs replaced the original norito—in which the heavenly and earthly sins contain discriminatory language toward the disabled and other groups—with a truncated text known as the '''Nakatomi Saibun'''.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/kaihatsu/oharai/theme_b.html|title=中臣祓の実践と注釈|publisher=國學院大學 伝統文化リサーチセンター|access-date=2025-04-24}} The modern ritual uses a slightly revised form of this prayer. == Court observances == [[File:Ceremony of the Enthronement of Emperor Shōwa in Shishinden Hall 4.jpg|thumb|right|The enthronement of Emperor Shōwa. Before the ''Ōmikuma-kujin-no-gi'' of the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]], the emperor performs ablutions and the Ō-harae.]] {{See also|Kaijo (ceremony)}} Under the [[:en:Taihō Code|Taihō Code]] of 701, Ō-harae became part of the formal court calendar, with detailed procedures later recorded in the ''Engishiki''. Documents such as ''Gishiki'', ''Hokuzanshō'', and ''E-ke Shidai'' describe the early ceremonies, and the ''Nihon Shoki'' records that in 676 (Tenmu 5) a grand purification ('''Ō-kaijo''') was held in which provincial governors presented horses, cloth, and hemp. The ''Yōrō Code'' prescribes that on the last days of the Sixth and Twelfth Months the Nakatomi present purge-hemp, the court scribes (''Fubito-be'') offer purge-sabres, and at the purification ground—usually before the [[:en:Suzakumon|Suzaku Gate]]—the Nakatomi proclaim the Ō-harae norito to the gathered officials while the diviners (''Urabe'') perform the rites. The ceremony lapsed after the [[:en:Ōnin War|Ōnin War]] devastated Kyoto. In 1871 (Meiji 4) Emperor Meiji revived the rite at the {{ill|Kashiko-dono|de|Kashiko-dono|ja|賢所|1=Kashiko-dokoro|2=ja|3=賢所|4=fr|5=Kashiko-dokoro|zh|賢所|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashiko-dono|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashiko-dokoro|qq=}} of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]], and the following year a proclamation ordered its restoration nationwide.''Nen-chū Gyōji Jiten'' (Encyclopedia of Annual Rites), Tokyo-dō Shuppan, 1958, p. 121. Since the adoption of the Western calendar in 1873, the court has observed the rite on 30 June and 31 December. The ceremony was duly performed for the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]] in the Taishō, Shōwa, and Heisei eras. In 2014 the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]], noting the decline in adult male princes, announced that henceforth adult female royals could also attend the rite.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.sankei.com/article/20140610- 000 |title=6月・12月「大祓の儀」ご参列　女性皇族にも拡大|publisher=産経ニュース|date=2014-06-10|access-date=2025-04-24}} == Popular observance == [[File:Ohyamato-jinja02s3200.jpg|thumb|right|A chinowa ring at [[:en:Ōyamato Shrine|Ōyamato Shrine]]]] Among the populace, the ceremonies have long been observed as rites of expiation: the Sixth-Month rite is commonly called '''Nagoshi-no-Harae''' (“summer purification”) and the Twelfth-Month rite '''Toshikoshi-no-Harae''' (“year-end purification”). Local variations include holding the ritual one month later (31 July) to match the lunar calendar. === Nagoshi-no-Harae === The ''Shūi Wakashū'' already contains an anonymous poem: "On Nagoshi-no-Harae in the Month of Waterless Moon, those who purify themselves are said to prolong their lives a thousand years." In an age when laundering clothes daily and abundant clean water were luxuries, replacing garments before the humid summer months was thought to ward off disease. The date also marks the end of the rainy season in most regions, a time to steel oneself for the coming heat and drought. After the rite fell into abeyance at court, it survived only in a few shrines and, from 1691 (Genroku 4), in limited form under names such as "Nagoshi Shinji".[[:en:Matsunoo Taisha|Matsuo Shrine]] official site, "Ōharae-shiki". The 1871 proclamation restoring Ō-harae nationwide also discouraged alternative names, but in the post-war era terms like "Nagoshi Shinji" have again come into use. ==== Passing through the Chinowa ==== At many shrines the highlight of Nagoshi-no-Harae is passing through a great ring of cogon grass (''chinowa''). A hoop several metres in diameter is set up in the approach, often within a rope-enclosed sacred space. Parishioners walk through it left, right, and left again in a figure-eight, thereby shedding the ailments and defilements of the past six months. In bygone days people wore small rings of grass on the body. This custom derives from the legend of [[:en:Somin Shōrai|Somin Shōrai]] in the [[:en:Bingo (American version)|Bingo Province]] fragment: the deity Mutō no Kami (identified with [[:en:Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo-no-Mikoto]]) instructed Somin-shōrai to wear a ring of grass to escape a plague. Some shrines dismantle the ring afterwards and allow worshippers to take pieces home, but a 2011 article in the ''Kyoto Shimbun'' cautioned that the grass has absorbed the participants’ defilements and should not be removed.''Kyoto Shimbun'', 24 June 2011, p. 24. Variants include the triple ring of cedar, pine, and sakaki at [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiwa Shrine]] in Nara, and the "U-shaped" chinowa of [[:en:Izumo-taisha|Izumo Taisha]], which worshippers leap over while discarding a bundle of grass from their shoulders.''Izumo Taishakyō Bukkyōshi Yōsei Kōshūkai'', Izumo Taishakyō Headquarters, 1989, p. 331. The custom has even been extended to pets, especially dogs.Aloha Street, "Chinowa and Pet Purification at Hawaii Kotohira Shrine & Hawai‘i Dazaifu Tenmangū", 2019. {{Commonscat|Chinowa|茅の輪}} === Use of ''Hitogata'' Paper Figures === Another practice is to breathe upon or rub a small human-shaped paper doll (''hitogata'') to transfer one’s impurities, then cast it into a river or the sea. Such dolls, and later {{ill|Tanzaku|de|Tanzaku|ja|短冊|zh|短冊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tanzaku|qq=}} inscribed at the [[:en:Qixi Festival|Tanabata]] festival, were occasionally burnt, a custom influenced by [[:en:Sagichō Fire Festival|Dondoyaki]] bonfires and esoteric Buddhist rites. === Food customs === In Kyoto it is customary to eat the confection '''{{ill|Minazuki (sweet)|de|Minazuki (Süßspeise)|ja|水無月 (和菓子)|zh|水無月 (菓子)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minazuki (sweet)|qq=}}'''—triangular ''u­i­ro­u'' topped with adzuki beans that symbolise ice and repel evil.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://ja.kyoto.travel/event/season/june/|title=夏越の祓|publisher=京都市観光協会|access-date=2025-04-24}} Since 2015 a promotional "'''Nagoshi Gohan'''"—a bowl of multigrain rice topped with a round fritter of summer vegetables—has been advocated by the public organisation "MAFF Net" to mark the occasion.''Yomiuri Shimbun'', 26 June 2015. In parts of [[:en:Kōchi Prefecture|Kōchi Prefecture]], the rite is nicknamed "'''Wanuke-sama'''" ("Passing-through-the-Ring"). == Notes == {{Notelist}} == References == {{Reflist|2}} == See also == * {{ill|Setsubiki|de|Setsubiki|ja|節折|1=Yoori|2=ja|3=節折|4=fr|5=Yoori|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|zh|節折|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Setsubiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=}} * [[:en:Garland|Garland]] == External links == * {{Kotobank|大祓}} {{translated page|ja|大祓|version=103420033|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| {{draft categories| [[Category:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace]] [[Category:Festivals in Japan]] [[Category:Exorcism in Shinto]] [[Category:Ritual purification]] [[Category:Shinto_festivals]] [[Category:Onmyōdō]] [[Category:Shinbutsu_shūgō]] [[Category:Lunisolar June]] [[Category:Japanese Lunar Calendar]] [[Category:Lunisolar December]] [[Category:japanese Lunar Calendar]] [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[ja:大祓]] [[sn:Ōharae-shiki]] [[sn:大祓]] [[en:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ar:Ōharae-shiki]] [[de:Ooharae]] [[Category:December]] [[Category:June]] [[Category:Buddhist holidays]] [[Category:夏の季語]] [[Category:Annual events in Japan]] [[Category:Japanese Imperial Rituals]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Shinto festivals]] [[Category:除災]] [[Category:雑節]] {{Commons category|Ōharae}} [[fr:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ko:오하라에]] {{Commons category|Ōharae}} [[fr:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ko:오하라에]] [[Category:translated pages with valid en interwikis]]

Before the ''Ōmikuma-kujin-no-gi'' of the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]], the emperor performs ablutions and the Ō-harae.]] {{See also|Kaijo (ceremony)}} Under the [[:en:Taihō Code|Taihō Code]] of 701, Ō-harae became part of the formal court calendar, with detailed procedures later recorded in the ''Engishiki''. Documents such as ''Gishiki'', ''Hokuzanshō'', and ''E-ke Shidai'' describe the early ceremonies, and the ''Nihon Shoki'' records that in 676 (Tenmu 5) a grand purification ('''Ō-kaijo''') was held in which provincial governors presented horses, cloth, and hemp. The ''Yōrō Code'' prescribes that on the last days of the Sixth and Twelfth Months the Nakatomi present purge-hemp, the court scribes (''Fubito-be'') offer purge-sabres, and at the purification ground—usually before the [[:en:Suzakumon|Suzaku Gate]]—the Nakatomi proclaim the Ō-harae norito to the gathered officials while the diviners (''Urabe'') perform the rites. The ceremony lapsed after the [[:en:Ōnin War|Ōnin War]] devastated Kyoto. In 1871 (Meiji 4) Emperor Meiji revived the rite at the {{ill|Kashiko-dono|de|Kashiko-dono|ja|賢所|1=Kashiko-dokoro|2=ja|3=賢所|4=fr|5=Kashiko-dokoro|zh|賢所|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashiko-dono|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashiko-dokoro|qq=}} of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]], and the following year a proclamation ordered its restoration nationwide.''Nen-chū Gyōji Jiten'' (Encyclopedia of Annual Rites), Tokyo-dō Shuppan, 1958, p. 121. Since the adoption of the Western calendar in 1873, the court has observed the rite on 30 June and 31 December. The ceremony was duly performed for the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]] in the Taishō, Shōwa, and Heisei eras. In 2014 the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]], noting the decline in adult male princes, announced that henceforth adult female royals could also attend the rite.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.sankei.com/article/20140610- 000 |title=6月・12月「大祓の儀」ご参列　女性皇族にも拡大|publisher=産経ニュース|date=2014-06-10|access-date=2025-04-24}} == Popular observance == [[File:Ohyamato-jinja02s3200.jpg|thumb|right|A chinowa ring at [[:en:Ōyamato Shrine|Ōyamato Shrine]]]] Among the populace, the ceremonies have long been observed as rites of expiation: the Sixth-Month rite is commonly called '''Nagoshi-no-Harae''' (“summer purification”) and the Twelfth-Month rite '''Toshikoshi-no-Harae''' (“year-end purification”). Local variations include holding the ritual one month later (31 July) to match the lunar calendar. === Nagoshi-no-Harae === The ''Shūi Wakashū'' already contains an anonymous poem: "On Nagoshi-no-Harae in the Month of Waterless Moon, those who purify themselves are said to prolong their lives a thousand years." In an age when laundering clothes daily and abundant clean water were luxuries, replacing garments before the humid summer months was thought to ward off disease. The date also marks the end of the rainy season in most regions, a time to steel oneself for the coming heat and drought. After the rite fell into abeyance at court, it survived only in a few shrines and, from 1691 (Genroku 4), in limited form under names such as "Nagoshi Shinji".[[:en:Matsunoo Taisha|Matsuo Shrine]] official site, "Ōharae-shiki". The 1871 proclamation restoring Ō-harae nationwide also discouraged alternative names, but in the post-war era terms like "Nagoshi Shinji" have again come into use. ==== Passing through the Chinowa ==== At many shrines the highlight of Nagoshi-no-Harae is passing through a great ring of cogon grass (''chinowa''). A hoop several metres in diameter is set up in the approach, often within a rope-enclosed sacred space. Parishioners walk through it left, right, and left again in a figure-eight, thereby shedding the ailments and defilements of the past six months. In bygone days people wore small rings of grass on the body. This custom derives from the legend of [[:en:Somin Shōrai|Somin Shōrai]] in the [[:en:Bingo (American version)|Bingo Province]] fragment: the deity Mutō no Kami (identified with [[:en:Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo-no-Mikoto]]) instructed Somin-shōrai to wear a ring of grass to escape a plague. Some shrines dismantle the ring afterwards and allow worshippers to take pieces home, but a 2011 article in the ''Kyoto Shimbun'' cautioned that the grass has absorbed the participants’ defilements and should not be removed.''Kyoto Shimbun'', 24 June 2011, p. 24. Variants include the triple ring of cedar, pine, and sakaki at [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiwa Shrine]] in Nara, and the "U-shaped" chinowa of [[:en:Izumo-taisha|Izumo Taisha]], which worshippers leap over while discarding a bundle of grass from their shoulders.''Izumo Taishakyō Bukkyōshi Yōsei Kōshūkai'', Izumo Taishakyō Headquarters, 1989, p. 331. The custom has even been extended to pets, especially dogs.Aloha Street, "Chinowa and Pet Purification at Hawaii Kotohira Shrine & Hawai‘i Dazaifu Tenmangū", 2019. {{Commonscat|Chinowa|茅の輪}} === Use of ''Hitogata'' Paper Figures === Another practice is to breathe upon or rub a small human-shaped paper doll (''hitogata'') to transfer one’s impurities, then cast it into a river or the sea. Such dolls, and later {{ill|Tanzaku|de|Tanzaku|ja|短冊|zh|短冊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tanzaku|qq=}} inscribed at the [[:en:Qixi Festival|Tanabata]] festival, were occasionally burnt, a custom influenced by [[:en:Sagichō Fire Festival|Dondoyaki]] bonfires and esoteric Buddhist rites. === Food customs === In Kyoto it is customary to eat the confection '''{{ill|Minazuki (sweet)|de|Minazuki (Süßspeise)|ja|水無月 (和菓子)|zh|水無月 (菓子)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minazuki (sweet)|qq=}}'''—triangular ''u­i­ro­u'' topped with adzuki beans that symbolise ice and repel evil.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://ja.kyoto.travel/event/season/june/|title=夏越の祓|publisher=京都市観光協会|access-date=2025-04-24}} Since 2015 a promotional "'''Nagoshi Gohan'''"—a bowl of multigrain rice topped with a round fritter of summer vegetables—has been advocated by the public organisation "MAFF Net" to mark the occasion.''Yomiuri Shimbun'', 26 June 2015. In parts of [[:en:Kōchi Prefecture|Kōchi Prefecture]], the rite is nicknamed "'''Wanuke-sama'''" ("Passing-through-the-Ring"). == Notes == {{Notelist}} == References == {{Reflist|2}} == See also == * {{ill|Setsubiki|de|Setsubiki|ja|節折|1=Yoori|2=ja|3=節折|4=fr|5=Yoori|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|zh|節折|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Setsubiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=}} * [[:en:Garland|Garland]] == External links == * {{Kotobank|大祓}} {{translated page|ja|大祓|version=103420033|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| {{draft categories| [[Category:Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace]] [[Category:Festivals in Japan]] [[Category:Exorcism in Shinto]] [[Category:Ritual purification]] [[Category:Shinto_festivals]] [[Category:Onmyōdō]] [[Category:Shinbutsu_shūgō]] [[Category:Lunisolar June]] [[Category:Japanese Lunar Calendar]] [[Category:Lunisolar December]] [[Category:japanese Lunar Calendar]] [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[ja:大祓]] [[sn:Ōharae-shiki]] [[sn:大祓]] [[en:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ar:Ōharae-shiki]] [[de:Ooharae]] [[Category:December]] [[Category:June]] [[Category:Buddhist holidays]] [[Category:夏の季語]] [[Category:Annual events in Japan]] [[Category:Japanese Imperial Rituals]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Shinto festivals]] [[Category:除災]] [[Category:雑節]] {{Commons category|Ōharae}} [[fr:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ko:오하라에]] {{Commons category|Ōharae}} [[fr:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ko:오하라에]] [[Category:translated pages with valid en interwikis]]

{{Lunisolar December}} {{Lunisolar June}} {{Short description|Japanese purification rite and festival}} {{Expand Japanese|大祓|date=November 2023}} {{Use dmy dates|date=December 2023}} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} The {{Nihongo|2=大祓式|3='''Ōharae-shiki'''}} is one of the [[Shinto]] purification rituals known as ''[[harae]]'' and is sometimes translated as "Great Purification".{{Cite web |last=Namiki |first=Kazuko |title=Ōharae |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9119 |access-date=9 November 2023 |website=[[Kokugakuin University]] Encyclopedia of Shinto}} It is also known as the {{Nihongo|2=中臣の祓|3=Nakatomi no harae}}. The ''[[Oharae no Kotoba|Ōharae no Kotoba]]'' prayer is recited during the ritual. The ritual is performed biannually on June 30{{Cite web |title=Nagoshi no Oharae Purification Ritual |url=https://www.kamigamojinja.jp/en/rituals/nagoshi-no-oharae-purification-ritual/ |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Kamo Wakeikazuchi Jinja Shrine (Kamigamo Jinja) |language=ja}} and December 30{{Cite web |last=Meador |first=Spencer |date=2017-07-04 |title=Oharae |url=http://sanpai-japan.com/2017/07/04/oharae/ |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Sanpai Japan |language=en-US}} at several shrines, but also as necessary, such as after an offense is committed, at the [[Daijosai]], or when an unmarried prince or princess departs the imperial palace to visit [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]] or the [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrines]].{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016-11-11 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-062171-1 |edition=Illustrated |location=New York (N.Y.) |language=English}}{{rp|7}} The December 30 ritual is sometimes held on New Year's Eve.{{Cite web |title=Shiwasu Oharae-shiki (Great Purification Ceremony in December) {{!}} Samukawa-jinja Shrine |url=https://samukawajinjya.jp/en/festival/shiwasuoharae.html |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Samukawa-jinja Shrine Official Website |language=en}} == History == The primary theory is that the ''Ōharae-shiki'' began at the end of the seventh century. It evolved over time, especially through the fifteenth century. These changes were linked to modifications to the [[Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]], a set of laws and rules, in the eighth century. The ''Ōharae-shiki'' changed again in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] (1603–1868), and some previous aspects were reestablished during the [[Meiji era|Meiji period]] (1868–1912). Purification became more important to prepare for this ritual and {{ill|Yoori|ja|節折|1=Yoori|2=ja|3=節折|4=fr|5=Yoori|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=}} became more prominent in the Meiji restoration.{{rp|362}}{{Clarify|date=January 2025|reason=This ritual is already for purification. Did other purification became more important? What is Yoori?}} == ''Minazuki-barae'' == Though the ''Ōharae-shiki'' conducted in June is sometimes confused with the {{Nihongo|2=水無月祓|3=Minazuki-barae}}—another purification rite that takes place at that time in the imperial court—they are conducted separately. ==Notelist== {{Notelist}} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Authority control}} {{citation needed}} {{citation needed}} {{Japanese Lunisolar Calendar}} ==Overview== {{Infobox Holiday | holiday_name = '''Ōharae''' (大祓) | type = Asian holiday | longtype = [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] rite | image = Ooharae-chinowa,katori-jingu,katori-city,japan.JPG | caption = A {{ill|Chinowa|de|Chinowa|ja|茅の輪|zh|茅之輪|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chinowa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓}} ring set up on the approach at [[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Shrine]] | official_name = Ōharae | nickname = Nagoshi-no-Harae, Natsu-Harae, Nagoshi, Minazuki-Harae | date = 30 June (Gregorian)
30 Sixth Month (lunisolar) | celebrations = Passing through the ''chinowa'', use of ''hitogata'' paper figures | relatedto = {{ill|Toshikoshi no Harae|de|Toshikoshi no Harae|ja|年越の祓|zh|年越之祓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toshikoshi no Harae|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} }} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} '''Ōharae''' (おおはらえ・おおはらい) is one of the major rites of [[:en:Harae|Harae]] in the [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] tradition of [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Grounded in the traditional Japanese concern for ritual purity, it aims to cleanse the mind and body of defilements (''kegare'') and remove the various sins and errors that give rise to misfortune, so that people may live each day with a pure and tranquil heart.{{Cite book|language=ja|title=神道いろは―神社とまつりの基礎知識―|date=2007-01-25|publisher=神社新報社|page=116|editor={{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|de|Jinja-honchō|ja|神社本庁教学研究所|zh|神社本庁教学研究所|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Association of Shinto Shrines|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}}} While purification rites (''harae'') are performed routinely at the {{ill|Imperial Court|de|Japanischer Kaiserhof|ja|宮中|zh|日本皇宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Court|qq=}} and in [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]], the twice-yearly ceremonies held for the benefit of all under heaven are distinguished by the name '''Ō-harae''' (“great purification”).''Sekai Daihyakka-jiten'' 2nd ed., s.v. "Ōharae". By long custom the rite is observed on the last day of the Sixth and Twelfth Months—that is, 30 June and 31 December in the modern calendar. In former times it was also conducted ad hoc, for example before and after the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]] (the first ''Niiname-sai'' after an [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor of Japan]]’s accession), in response to unprecedented epidemics or disasters, or to purify candidates for the offices of [[:en:Saikū|Saigū]] and [[:en:Saiin (priestess)|Saiin]]. The ceremony is also called the "Purification of the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]]" ('''Nakatomi-no-Harae'''). == Overview == The earliest textual attestation appears in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], in the section on [[:en:Emperor Chūai|Emperor Chūai]]: {{quote|Take also the great offerings (''Ō-nusa'') of the land and perform a '''great purification''', removing the sins of raw-hide flaying, reverse flaying, dam-filling, dung-gate, incest, bestiality with horse, ox, fowl, and dog…|Adapted from the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], Chūai no Maki}} These offences are collectively known as [[:en:Tsumi|Heavenly sins and earthly sins]]. {{Lunisolar December}} {{Lunisolar June}} {{Short description|Japanese purification rite and festival}} {{Expand Japanese|大祓|date=November 2023}} {{Use dmy dates|date=December 2023}} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} The {{Nihongo|2=大祓式|3='''Ōharae-shiki'''}} is one of the [[Shinto]] purification rituals known as ''[[harae]]'' and is sometimes translated as "Great Purification".{{Cite web |last=Namiki |first=Kazuko |title=Ōharae |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9119 |access-date=9 November 2023 |website=[[Kokugakuin University]] Encyclopedia of Shinto}} It is also known as the {{Nihongo|2=中臣の祓|3=Nakatomi no harae}}. The ''[[Oharae no Kotoba|Ōharae no Kotoba]]'' prayer is recited during the ritual. The ritual is performed biannually on June 30{{Cite web |title=Nagoshi no Oharae Purification Ritual |url=https://www.kamigamojinja.jp/en/rituals/nagoshi-no-oharae-purification-ritual/ |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Kamo Wakeikazuchi Jinja Shrine (Kamigamo Jinja) |language=ja}} and December 30{{Cite web |last=Meador |first=Spencer |date=2017-07-04 |title=Oharae |url=http://sanpai-japan.com/2017/07/04/oharae/ |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Sanpai Japan |language=en-US}} at several shrines, but also as necessary, such as after an offense is committed, at the [[Daijosai]], or when an unmarried prince or princess departs the imperial palace to visit [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]] or the [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrines]].{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016-11-11 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-062171-1 |edition=Illustrated |location=New York (N.Y.) |language=English}}{{rp|7}} The December 30 ritual is sometimes held on New Year's Eve.{{Cite web |title=Shiwasu Oharae-shiki (Great Purification Ceremony in December) {{!}} Samukawa-jinja Shrine |url=https://samukawajinjya.jp/en/festival/shiwasuoharae.html |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Samukawa-jinja Shrine Official Website |language=en}} == History == The primary theory is that the ''Ōharae-shiki'' began at the end of the seventh century. It evolved over time, especially through the fifteenth century. These changes were linked to modifications to the [[Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]], a set of laws and rules, in the eighth century. The ''Ōharae-shiki'' changed again in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] (1603–1868), and some previous aspects were reestablished during the [[Meiji era|Meiji period]] (1868–1912). Purification became more important to prepare for this ritual and {{ill|Yoori|ja|節折|1=Yoori|2=ja|3=節折|4=fr|5=Yoori|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=}} became more prominent in the Meiji restoration.{{rp|362}}{{Clarify|date=January 2025|reason=This ritual is already for purification. Did other purification became more important? What is Yoori?}} == ''Minazuki-barae'' == Though the ''Ōharae-shiki'' conducted in June is sometimes confused with the {{Nihongo|2=水無月祓|3=Minazuki-barae}}—another purification rite that takes place at that time in the imperial court—they are conducted separately. ==Notelist== {{Notelist}} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Authority control}} {{citation needed}} {{citation needed}} {{Japanese Lunisolar Calendar}} ==Overview== {{Infobox Holiday | holiday_name = '''Ōharae''' (大祓) | type = Asian holiday | longtype = [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] rite | image = Ooharae-chinowa,katori-jingu,katori-city,japan.JPG | caption = A {{ill|Chinowa|de|Chinowa|ja|茅の輪|zh|茅之輪|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chinowa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓}} ring set up on the approach at [[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Shrine]] | official_name = Ōharae | nickname = Nagoshi-no-Harae, Natsu-Harae, Nagoshi, Minazuki-Harae | date = 30 June (Gregorian)
30 Sixth Month (lunisolar) | celebrations = Passing through the ''chinowa'', use of ''hitogata'' paper figures | relatedto = {{ill|Toshikoshi no Harae|de|Toshikoshi no Harae|ja|年越の祓|zh|年越之祓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toshikoshi no Harae|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} }} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} '''Ōharae''' (おおはらえ・おおはらい) is one of the major rites of [[:en:Harae|Harae]] in the [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] tradition of [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Grounded in the traditional Japanese concern for ritual purity, it aims to cleanse the mind and body of defilements (''kegare'') and remove the various sins and errors that give rise to misfortune, so that people may live each day with a pure and tranquil heart.{{Cite book|language=ja|title=神道いろは―神社とまつりの基礎知識―|date=2007-01-25|publisher=神社新報社|page=116|editor={{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|de|Jinja-honchō|ja|神社本庁教学研究所|zh|神社本庁教学研究所|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Association of Shinto Shrines|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}}} While purification rites (''harae'') are performed routinely at the {{ill|Imperial Court|de|Japanischer Kaiserhof|ja|宮中|zh|日本皇宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Court|qq=}} and in [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]], the twice-yearly ceremonies held for the benefit of all under heaven are distinguished by the name '''Ō-harae''' (“great purification”).''Sekai Daihyakka-jiten'' 2nd ed., s.v. "Ōharae". By long custom the rite is observed on the last day of the Sixth and Twelfth Months—that is, 30 June and 31 December in the modern calendar. In former times it was also conducted ad hoc, for example before and after the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]] (the first ''Niiname-sai'' after an [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor of Japan]]’s accession), in response to unprecedented epidemics or disasters, or to purify candidates for the offices of [[:en:Saikū|Saigū]] and [[:en:Saiin (priestess)|Saiin]]. The ceremony is also called the "Purification of the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]]" ('''Nakatomi-no-Harae'''). == Overview == The earliest textual attestation appears in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], in the section on [[:en:Emperor Chūai|Emperor Chūai]]: {{quote|Take also the great offerings (''Ō-nusa'') of the land and perform a '''great purification''', removing the sins of raw-hide flaying, reverse flaying, dam-filling, dung-gate, incest, bestiality with horse, ox, fowl, and dog…|Adapted from the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], Chūai no Maki}} These offences are collectively known as [[:en:Tsumi|Heavenly sins and earthly sins]]. Because ordinary sins (''tsumi'') and ritual defilements (''kegare'') could not be removed by the short everyday formulas (''harae-kotoba''), the lengthy '''Ō-harae Norito''' was proclaimed to cleanse them. The prayer lists the heavenly sins, which largely concern violations of agricultural taboos, before the earthly sins, implying that in ancient times the former were seen as the graver threat to communal order. Originally the texts for the Sixth- and Twelfth-Month rites differed, but the [[:en:Engishiki|Engishiki]] notes "The Twelfth-Month rite shall follow the precedent of the Sixth," so only the Sixth-Month version survives. While today the norito is recited to the kami, the version in the ''Engishiki'' makes clear that the officiant first calls upon the assembled participants to listen, they respond "Ō" (''isshō''), and only then follows the mythic preamble, enumeration of sins, and description of how the {{ill|Haraedo no Kami|de|Haraedo-no-kami|ja|祓戸大神|zh|祓戶大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haraedo no Kami|qq=}} carry them away. Thus Ō-harae not only "resets" calamities that have already occurred and prays for the tranquillity of the realm, it also functioned as a public proclamation of the taboos imposed by the ruling authority.''Sekai Daihyakka-jiten'', 2nd ed., s.v. "Kodai-hō" (ancient law). In 1914 (Taishō 3) the Ministry of Home Affairs replaced the original norito—in which the heavenly and earthly sins contain discriminatory language toward the disabled and other groups—with a truncated text known as the '''Nakatomi Saibun'''.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/kaihatsu/oharai/theme_b.html|title=中臣祓の実践と注釈|publisher=國學院大學 伝統文化リサーチセンター|access-date=2025-04-24}} The modern ritual uses a slightly revised form of this prayer. == Court observances == [[File:Ceremony of the Enthronement of Emperor Shōwa in Shishinden Hall 4.jpg|thumb|right|The enthronement of Emperor Shōwa. Before the ''Ōmikuma-kujin-no-gi'' of the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]], the emperor performs ablutions and the Ō-harae.]] {{See also|Kaijo (ceremony)}} Under the [[:en:Taihō Code|Taihō Code]] of 701, Ō-harae became part of the formal court calendar, with detailed procedures later recorded in the ''Engishiki''. Documents such as ''Gishiki'', ''Hokuzanshō'', and ''E-ke Shidai'' describe the early ceremonies, and the ''Nihon Shoki'' records that in 676 (Tenmu 5) a grand purification ('''Ō-kaijo''') was held in which provincial governors presented horses, cloth, and hemp. The ''Yōrō Code'' prescribes that on the last days of the Sixth and Twelfth Months the Nakatomi present purge-hemp, the court scribes (''Fubito-be'') offer purge-sabres, and at the purification ground—usually before the [[:en:Suzakumon|Suzaku Gate]]—the Nakatomi proclaim the Ō-harae norito to the gathered officials while the diviners (''Urabe'') perform the rites. The ceremony lapsed after the [[:en:Ōnin War|Ōnin War]] devastated Kyoto. In 1871 (Meiji 4) Emperor Meiji revived the rite at the {{ill|Kashiko-dono|de|Kashiko-dono|ja|賢所|1=Kashiko-dokoro|2=ja|3=賢所|4=fr|5=Kashiko-dokoro|zh|賢所|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashiko-dono|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashiko-dokoro|qq=}} of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]], and the following year a proclamation ordered its restoration nationwide.''Nen-chū Gyōji Jiten'' (Encyclopedia of Annual Rites), Tokyo-dō Shuppan, 1958, p. 121. Since the adoption of the Western calendar in 1873, the court has observed the rite on 30 June and 31 December. The ceremony was duly performed for the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]] in the Taishō, Shōwa, and Heisei eras. In 2014 the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]], noting the decline in adult male princes, announced that henceforth adult female royals could also attend the rite.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.sankei.com/article/20140610- 000 |title=6月・12月「大祓の儀」ご参列　女性皇族にも拡大|publisher=産経ニュース|date=2014-06-10|access-date=2025-04-24}} == Popular observance == [[File:Ohyamato-jinja02s3200.jpg|thumb|right|A chinowa ring at [[:en:Ōyamato Shrine|Ōyamato Shrine]]]] Among the populace, the ceremonies have long been observed as rites of expiation: the Sixth-Month rite is commonly called '''Nagoshi-no-Harae''' (“summer purification”) and the Twelfth-Month rite '''Toshikoshi-no-Harae''' (“year-end purification”). Local variations include holding the ritual one month later (31 July) to match the lunar calendar. === Nagoshi-no-Harae === The ''Shūi Wakashū'' already contains an anonymous poem: "On Nagoshi-no-Harae in the Month of Waterless Moon, those who purify themselves are said to prolong their lives a thousand years." In an age when laundering clothes daily and abundant clean water were luxuries, replacing garments before the humid summer months was thought to ward off disease. The date also marks the end of the rainy season in most regions, a time to steel oneself for the coming heat and drought. After the rite fell into abeyance at court, it survived only in a few shrines and, from 1691 (Genroku 4), in limited form under names such as "Nagoshi Shinji".[[:en:Matsunoo Taisha|Matsuo Shrine]] official site, "Ōharae-shiki". The 1871 proclamation restoring Ō-harae nationwide also discouraged alternative names, but in the post-war era terms like "Nagoshi Shinji" have again come into use. ==== Passing through the Chinowa ==== At many shrines the highlight of Nagoshi-no-Harae is passing through a great ring of cogon grass (''chinowa''). A hoop several metres in diameter is set up in the approach, often within a rope-enclosed sacred space. Parishioners walk through it left, right, and left again in a figure-eight, thereby shedding the ailments and defilements of the past six months. In bygone days people wore small rings of grass on the body. This custom derives from the legend of [[:en:Somin Shōrai|Somin Shōrai]] in the [[:en:Bingo (American version)|Bingo Province]] fragment: the deity Mutō no Kami (identified with [[:en:Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo-no-Mikoto]]) instructed Somin-shōrai to wear a ring of grass to escape a plague. Some shrines dismantle the ring afterwards and allow worshippers to take pieces home, but a 2011 article in the ''Kyoto Shimbun'' cautioned that the grass has absorbed the participants’ defilements and should not be removed.''Kyoto Shimbun'', 24 June 2011, p. 24. Variants include the triple ring of cedar, pine, and sakaki at [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiwa Shrine]] in Nara, and the "U-shaped" chinowa of [[:en:Izumo-taisha|Izumo Taisha]], which worshippers leap over while discarding a bundle of grass from their shoulders.''Izumo Taishakyō Bukkyōshi Yōsei Kōshūkai'', Izumo Taishakyō Headquarters, 1989, p. 331. The custom has even been extended to pets, especially dogs.Aloha Street, "Chinowa and Pet Purification at Hawaii Kotohira Shrine & Hawai‘i Dazaifu Tenmangū", 2019. {{Commonscat|Chinowa|茅の輪}} === Use of ''Hitogata'' Paper Figures === Another practice is to breathe upon or rub a small human-shaped paper doll (''hitogata'') to transfer one’s impurities, then cast it into a river or the sea. Such dolls, and later {{ill|Tanzaku|de|Tanzaku|ja|短冊|zh|短冊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tanzaku|qq=}} inscribed at the [[:en:Qixi Festival|Tanabata]] festival, were occasionally burnt, a custom influenced by [[:en:Sagichō Fire Festival|Dondoyaki]] bonfires and esoteric Buddhist rites. === Food customs === In Kyoto it is customary to eat the confection '''{{ill|Minazuki (sweet)|de|Minazuki (Süßspeise)|ja|水無月 (和菓子)|zh|水無月 (菓子)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minazuki (sweet)|qq=}}'''—triangular ''u­i­ro­u'' topped with adzuki beans that symbolise ice and repel evil.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://ja.kyoto.travel/event/season/june/|title=夏越の祓|publisher=京都市観光協会|access-date=2025-04-24}} Since 2015 a promotional "'''Nagoshi Gohan'''"—a bowl of multigrain rice topped with a round fritter of summer vegetables—has been advocated by the public organisation "MAFF Net" to mark the occasion.''Yomiuri Shimbun'', 26 June 2015. In parts of [[:en:Kōchi Prefecture|Kōchi Prefecture]], the rite is nicknamed "'''Wanuke-sama'''" ("Passing-through-the-Ring"). == Notes == {{Notelist}} == References == {{Reflist|2}} == See also == * {{ill|Setsubiki|de|Setsubiki|ja|節折|1=Yoori|2=ja|3=節折|4=fr|5=Yoori|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|zh|節折|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Setsubiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=}} * [[:en:Garland|Garland]] == External links == * {{Kotobank|大祓}} {{translated page|ja|大祓|version=103420033|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| {{draft categories| [[Category:Festivals in Japan]] [[Category:Exorcism in Shinto]] [[Category:Ritual purification]] [[Category:Shinto_festivals]] [[Category:Onmyōdō]] [[Category:Shinbutsu_shūgō]] [[Category:Lunisolar June]] [[Category:Japanese Lunar Calendar]] [[Category:Lunisolar December]] [[Category:japanese Lunar Calendar]] [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[ja:大祓]] [[sn:Ōharae-shiki]] [[sn:大祓]] [[en:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ar:Ōharae-shiki]] [[de:Ooharae]] [[Category:December]] [[Category:June]] [[Category:Buddhist holidays]] [[Category:夏の季語]] [[Category:Annual events in Japan]] [[Category:Japanese Imperial Rituals]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Shinto festivals]] [[Category:除災]] [[Category:雑節]] {{Commons category|Ōharae}} [[fr:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ko:오하라에]] {{Commons category|Ōharae}} [[fr:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ko:오하라에]] [[Category:translated pages with valid en interwikis]] [[Category:Japanese Imperial Rituals]]

Before the ''Ōmikuma-kujin-no-gi'' of the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]], the emperor performs ablutions and the Ō-harae.]] {{See also|Kaijo (ceremony)}} Under the [[:en:Taihō Code|Taihō Code]] of 701, Ō-harae became part of the formal court calendar, with detailed procedures later recorded in the ''Engishiki''. Documents such as ''Gishiki'', ''Hokuzanshō'', and ''E-ke Shidai'' describe the early ceremonies, and the ''Nihon Shoki'' records that in 676 (Tenmu 5) a grand purification ('''Ō-kaijo''') was held in which provincial governors presented horses, cloth, and hemp. The ''Yōrō Code'' prescribes that on the last days of the Sixth and Twelfth Months the Nakatomi present purge-hemp, the court scribes (''Fubito-be'') offer purge-sabres, and at the purification ground—usually before the [[:en:Suzakumon|Suzaku Gate]]—the Nakatomi proclaim the Ō-harae norito to the gathered officials while the diviners (''Urabe'') perform the rites. The ceremony lapsed after the [[:en:Ōnin War|Ōnin War]] devastated Kyoto. In 1871 (Meiji 4) Emperor Meiji revived the rite at the {{ill|Kashiko-dono|de|Kashiko-dono|ja|賢所|1=Kashiko-dokoro|2=ja|3=賢所|4=fr|5=Kashiko-dokoro|zh|賢所|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashiko-dono|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashiko-dokoro|qq=}} of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]], and the following year a proclamation ordered its restoration nationwide.''Nen-chū Gyōji Jiten'' (Encyclopedia of Annual Rites), Tokyo-dō Shuppan, 1958, p. 121. Since the adoption of the Western calendar in 1873, the court has observed the rite on 30 June and 31 December. The ceremony was duly performed for the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]] in the Taishō, Shōwa, and Heisei eras. In 2014 the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]], noting the decline in adult male princes, announced that henceforth adult female royals could also attend the rite.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.sankei.com/article/20140610- 000 |title=6月・12月「大祓の儀」ご参列　女性皇族にも拡大|publisher=産経ニュース|date=2014-06-10|access-date=2025-04-24}} == Popular observance == [[File:Ohyamato-jinja02s3200.jpg|thumb|right|A chinowa ring at [[:en:Ōyamato Shrine|Ōyamato Shrine]]]] Among the populace, the ceremonies have long been observed as rites of expiation: the Sixth-Month rite is commonly called '''Nagoshi-no-Harae''' (“summer purification”) and the Twelfth-Month rite '''Toshikoshi-no-Harae''' (“year-end purification”). Local variations include holding the ritual one month later (31 July) to match the lunar calendar. === Nagoshi-no-Harae === The ''Shūi Wakashū'' already contains an anonymous poem: "On Nagoshi-no-Harae in the Month of Waterless Moon, those who purify themselves are said to prolong their lives a thousand years." In an age when laundering clothes daily and abundant clean water were luxuries, replacing garments before the humid summer months was thought to ward off disease. The date also marks the end of the rainy season in most regions, a time to steel oneself for the coming heat and drought. After the rite fell into abeyance at court, it survived only in a few shrines and, from 1691 (Genroku 4), in limited form under names such as "Nagoshi Shinji".[[:en:Matsunoo Taisha|Matsuo Shrine]] official site, "Ōharae-shiki". The 1871 proclamation restoring Ō-harae nationwide also discouraged alternative names, but in the post-war era terms like "Nagoshi Shinji" have again come into use. ==== Passing through the Chinowa ==== At many shrines the highlight of Nagoshi-no-Harae is passing through a great ring of cogon grass (''chinowa''). A hoop several metres in diameter is set up in the approach, often within a rope-enclosed sacred space. Parishioners walk through it left, right, and left again in a figure-eight, thereby shedding the ailments and defilements of the past six months. In bygone days people wore small rings of grass on the body. This custom derives from the legend of [[:en:Somin Shōrai|Somin Shōrai]] in the [[:en:Bingo (American version)|Bingo Province]] fragment: the deity Mutō no Kami (identified with [[:en:Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo-no-Mikoto]]) instructed Somin-shōrai to wear a ring of grass to escape a plague. Some shrines dismantle the ring afterwards and allow worshippers to take pieces home, but a 2011 article in the ''Kyoto Shimbun'' cautioned that the grass has absorbed the participants’ defilements and should not be removed.''Kyoto Shimbun'', 24 June 2011, p. 24. Variants include the triple ring of cedar, pine, and sakaki at [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiwa Shrine]] in Nara, and the "U-shaped" chinowa of [[:en:Izumo-taisha|Izumo Taisha]], which worshippers leap over while discarding a bundle of grass from their shoulders.''Izumo Taishakyō Bukkyōshi Yōsei Kōshūkai'', Izumo Taishakyō Headquarters, 1989, p. 331. The custom has even been extended to pets, especially dogs.Aloha Street, "Chinowa and Pet Purification at Hawaii Kotohira Shrine & Hawai‘i Dazaifu Tenmangū", 2019. {{Commonscat|Chinowa|茅の輪}} === Use of ''Hitogata'' Paper Figures === Another practice is to breathe upon or rub a small human-shaped paper doll (''hitogata'') to transfer one’s impurities, then cast it into a river or the sea. Such dolls, and later {{ill|Tanzaku|de|Tanzaku|ja|短冊|zh|短冊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tanzaku|qq=}} inscribed at the [[:en:Qixi Festival|Tanabata]] festival, were occasionally burnt, a custom influenced by [[:en:Sagichō Fire Festival|Dondoyaki]] bonfires and esoteric Buddhist rites. === Food customs === In Kyoto it is customary to eat the confection '''{{ill|Minazuki (sweet)|de|Minazuki (Süßspeise)|ja|水無月 (和菓子)|zh|水無月 (菓子)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minazuki (sweet)|qq=}}'''—triangular ''u­i­ro­u'' topped with adzuki beans that symbolise ice and repel evil.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://ja.kyoto.travel/event/season/june/|title=夏越の祓|publisher=京都市観光協会|access-date=2025-04-24}} Since 2015 a promotional "'''Nagoshi Gohan'''"—a bowl of multigrain rice topped with a round fritter of summer vegetables—has been advocated by the public organisation "MAFF Net" to mark the occasion.''Yomiuri Shimbun'', 26 June 2015. In parts of [[:en:Kōchi Prefecture|Kōchi Prefecture]], the rite is nicknamed "'''Wanuke-sama'''" ("Passing-through-the-Ring"). == Notes == {{Notelist}} == References == {{Reflist|2}} == See also == * {{ill|Setsubiki|de|Setsubiki|ja|節折|1=Yoori|2=ja|3=節折|4=fr|5=Yoori|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|zh|節折|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Setsubiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=}} * [[:en:Garland|Garland]] == External links == * {{Kotobank|大祓}} {{translated page|ja|大祓|version=103420033|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| {{draft categories| [[Category:Festivals in Japan]] [[Category:Exorcism in Shinto]] [[Category:Ritual purification]] [[Category:Shinto_festivals]] [[Category:Onmyōdō]] [[Category:Shinbutsu_shūgō]] [[Category:Lunisolar June]] [[Category:Japanese Lunar Calendar]] [[Category:Lunisolar December]] [[Category:japanese Lunar Calendar]] [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[ja:大祓]] [[sn:Ōharae-shiki]] [[sn:大祓]] [[en:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ar:Ōharae-shiki]] [[de:Ooharae]] [[Category:December]] [[Category:June]] [[Category:Buddhist holidays]] [[Category:夏の季語]] [[Category:Annual events in Japan]] [[Category:Japanese Imperial Rituals]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Shinto festivals]] [[Category:除災]] [[Category:雑節]] {{Commons category|Ōharae}} [[fr:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ko:오하라에]] {{Commons category|Ōharae}} [[fr:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ko:오하라에]] [[Category:translated pages with valid en interwikis]] [[Category:Japanese Imperial Rituals]]

{{Lunisolar December}} {{Lunisolar June}} {{Short description|Japanese purification rite and festival}} {{Expand Japanese|大祓|date=November 2023}} {{Use dmy dates|date=December 2023}} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} The {{Nihongo|2=大祓式|3='''Ōharae-shiki'''}} is one of the [[Shinto]] purification rituals known as ''[[:en:Harae|Harae]]'' and is sometimes translated as "Great Purification".{{Cite web |last=Namiki |first=Kazuko |title=Ōharae |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9119 |access-date=9 November 2023 |website=[[Kokugakuin University]] Encyclopedia of Shinto}} It is also known as the {{Nihongo|2=中臣の祓|3=Nakatomi no harae}}. The ''[[Oharae no Kotoba|Ōharae no Kotoba]]'' prayer is recited during the ritual. The ritual is performed biannually on June 30{{Cite web |title=Nagoshi no Oharae Purification Ritual |url=https://www.kamigamojinja.jp/en/rituals/nagoshi-no-oharae-purification-ritual/ |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Kamo Wakeikazuchi Jinja Shrine (Kamigamo Jinja) |language=ja}} and December 30{{Cite web |last=Meador |first=Spencer |date=2017-07-04 |title=Oharae |url=http://sanpai-japan.com/2017/07/04/oharae/ |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Sanpai Japan |language=en-US}} at several shrines, but also as necessary, such as after an offense is committed, at the [[Daijosai]], or when an unmarried prince or princess departs the imperial palace to visit [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]] or the [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrines]].{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016-11-11 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-062171-1 |edition=Illustrated |location=New York (N.Y.) |language=English}}{{rp|7}} The December 30 ritual is sometimes held on New Year's Eve.{{Cite web |title=Shiwasu Oharae-shiki (Great Purification Ceremony in December) {{!}} Samukawa-jinja Shrine |url=https://samukawajinjya.jp/en/festival/shiwasuoharae.html |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Samukawa-jinja Shrine Official Website |language=en}} == History == The primary theory is that the ''Ōharae-shiki'' began at the end of the seventh century. It evolved over time, especially through the fifteenth century. These changes were linked to modifications to the [[Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]], a set of laws and rules, in the eighth century. The ''Ōharae-shiki'' changed again in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] (1603–1868), and some previous aspects were reestablished during the [[Meiji era|Meiji period]] (1868–1912). Purification became more important to prepare for this ritual and {{ill|Yoori|ja|節折|1=Yoori|2=ja|3=節折|4=fr|5=Yoori|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=}} became more prominent in the Meiji restoration.{{rp|362}}{{Clarify|date=January 2025|reason=This ritual is already for purification. Did other purification became more important? What is Yoori?}} == ''Minazuki-barae'' == Though the ''Ōharae-shiki'' conducted in June is sometimes confused with the {{Nihongo|2=水無月祓|3=Minazuki-barae}}—another purification rite that takes place at that time in the imperial court—they are conducted separately. ==Notelist== {{Notelist}} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Authority control}} {{citation needed}} {{citation needed}} {{Japanese Lunisolar Calendar}} ==Overview== {{Infobox Holiday | holiday_name = '''Ōharae''' (大祓) | type = Asian holiday | longtype = [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] rite | image = Ooharae-chinowa,katori-jingu,katori-city,japan.JPG | caption = A {{ill|Chinowa|de|Chinowa|ja|茅の輪|zh|茅之輪|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chinowa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓}} ring set up on the approach at [[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Shrine]] | official_name = Ōharae | nickname = Nagoshi-no-Harae, Natsu-Harae, Nagoshi, Minazuki-Harae | date = 30 June (Gregorian)
30 Sixth Month (lunisolar) | celebrations = Passing through the ''chinowa'', use of ''hitogata'' paper figures | relatedto = {{ill|Toshikoshi no Harae|de|Toshikoshi no Harae|ja|年越の祓|zh|年越之祓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toshikoshi no Harae|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} }} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} '''Ōharae''' (おおはらえ・おおはらい) is one of the major rites of [[:en:Harae|Harae]] in the [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] tradition of [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Grounded in the traditional Japanese concern for ritual purity, it aims to cleanse the mind and body of defilements (''kegare'') and remove the various sins and errors that give rise to misfortune, so that people may live each day with a pure and tranquil heart.{{Cite book|language=ja|title=神道いろは―神社とまつりの基礎知識―|date=2007-01-25|publisher=神社新報社|page=116|editor={{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|de|Jinja-honchō|ja|神社本庁教学研究所|zh|神社本庁教学研究所|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Association of Shinto Shrines|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}}} While purification rites (''harae'') are performed routinely at the {{ill|Imperial Court|de|Japanischer Kaiserhof|ja|宮中|zh|日本皇宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Court|qq=}} and in [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]], the twice-yearly ceremonies held for the benefit of all under heaven are distinguished by the name '''Ō-harae''' (“great purification”).''Sekai Daihyakka-jiten'' 2nd ed., s.v. "Ōharae". By long custom the rite is observed on the last day of the Sixth and Twelfth Months—that is, 30 June and 31 December in the modern calendar. In former times it was also conducted ad hoc, for example before and after the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]] (the first ''Niiname-sai'' after an [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor of Japan]]’s accession), in response to unprecedented epidemics or disasters, or to purify candidates for the offices of [[:en:Saikū|Saigū]] and [[:en:Saiin (priestess)|Saiin]]. The ceremony is also called the "Purification of the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]]" ('''Nakatomi-no-Harae'''). == Overview == The earliest textual attestation appears in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], in the section on [[:en:Emperor Chūai|Emperor Chūai]]: {{quote|Take also the great offerings (''Ō-nusa'') of the land and perform a '''great purification''', removing the sins of raw-hide flaying, reverse flaying, dam-filling, dung-gate, incest, bestiality with horse, ox, fowl, and dog…|Adapted from the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], Chūai no Maki}} These offences are collectively known as [[:en:Tsumi|Heavenly sins and earthly sins]]. While today the norito is recited to the kami, the version in the ''Engishiki'' makes clear that the officiant first calls upon the assembled participants to listen, they respond "Ō" (''isshō''), and only then follows the mythic preamble, enumeration of sins, and description of how the {{ill|Haraedo no Kami|de|Haraedo-no-kami|ja|祓戸大神|zh|祓戶大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haraedo no Kami|qq=}} carry them away. Thus Ō-harae not only "resets" calamities that have already occurred and prays for the tranquillity of the realm, it also functioned as a public proclamation of the taboos imposed by the ruling authority.''Sekai Daihyakka-jiten'', 2nd ed., s.v. {{Lunisolar December}} {{Lunisolar June}} {{Short description|Japanese purification rite and festival}} {{Expand Japanese|大祓|date=November 2023}} {{Use dmy dates|date=December 2023}} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} The {{Nihongo|2=大祓式|3='''Ōharae-shiki'''}} is one of the [[Shinto]] purification rituals known as ''[[:en:Harae|Harae]]'' and is sometimes translated as "Great Purification".{{Cite web |last=Namiki |first=Kazuko |title=Ōharae |url=https://d-museum.kokugakuin.ac.jp/eos/detail/?id=9119 |access-date=9 November 2023 |website=[[Kokugakuin University]] Encyclopedia of Shinto}} It is also known as the {{Nihongo|2=中臣の祓|3=Nakatomi no harae}}. The ''[[Oharae no Kotoba|Ōharae no Kotoba]]'' prayer is recited during the ritual. The ritual is performed biannually on June 30{{Cite web |title=Nagoshi no Oharae Purification Ritual |url=https://www.kamigamojinja.jp/en/rituals/nagoshi-no-oharae-purification-ritual/ |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Kamo Wakeikazuchi Jinja Shrine (Kamigamo Jinja) |language=ja}} and December 30{{Cite web |last=Meador |first=Spencer |date=2017-07-04 |title=Oharae |url=http://sanpai-japan.com/2017/07/04/oharae/ |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Sanpai Japan |language=en-US}} at several shrines, but also as necessary, such as after an offense is committed, at the [[Daijosai]], or when an unmarried prince or princess departs the imperial palace to visit [[Ise Grand Shrine|Ise Shrine]] or the [[Kamo shrines|Kamo Shrines]].{{Cite book |last=Hardacre |first=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016-11-11 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-062171-1 |edition=Illustrated |location=New York (N.Y.) |language=English}}{{rp|7}} The December 30 ritual is sometimes held on New Year's Eve.{{Cite web |title=Shiwasu Oharae-shiki (Great Purification Ceremony in December) {{!}} Samukawa-jinja Shrine |url=https://samukawajinjya.jp/en/festival/shiwasuoharae.html |access-date=2023-06-05 |website=Samukawa-jinja Shrine Official Website |language=en}} == History == The primary theory is that the ''Ōharae-shiki'' began at the end of the seventh century. It evolved over time, especially through the fifteenth century. These changes were linked to modifications to the [[Ritsuryō|Ritsuryō system]], a set of laws and rules, in the eighth century. The ''Ōharae-shiki'' changed again in the [[:en:Edo period|Edo period]] (1603–1868), and some previous aspects were reestablished during the [[Meiji era|Meiji period]] (1868–1912). Purification became more important to prepare for this ritual and {{ill|Yoori|ja|節折|1=Yoori|2=ja|3=節折|4=fr|5=Yoori|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=draft|qq=draft|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=}} became more prominent in the Meiji restoration.{{rp|362}}{{Clarify|date=January 2025|reason=This ritual is already for purification. Did other purification became more important? What is Yoori?}} == ''Minazuki-barae'' == Though the ''Ōharae-shiki'' conducted in June is sometimes confused with the {{Nihongo|2=水無月祓|3=Minazuki-barae}}—another purification rite that takes place at that time in the imperial court—they are conducted separately. ==Notelist== {{Notelist}} ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Authority control}} {{citation needed}} {{citation needed}} {{Japanese Lunisolar Calendar}} ==Overview== {{Infobox Holiday | holiday_name = '''Ōharae''' (大祓) | type = Asian holiday | longtype = [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] rite | image = Ooharae-chinowa,katori-jingu,katori-city,japan.JPG | caption = A {{ill|Chinowa|de|Chinowa|ja|茅の輪|zh|茅之輪|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Chinowa|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki redirects to 大祓}} ring set up on the approach at [[:en:Katori Shrine|Katori Shrine]] | official_name = Ōharae | nickname = Nagoshi-no-Harae, Natsu-Harae, Nagoshi, Minazuki-Harae | date = 30 June (Gregorian)
30 Sixth Month (lunisolar) | celebrations = Passing through the ''chinowa'', use of ''hitogata'' paper figures | relatedto = {{ill|Toshikoshi no Harae|de|Toshikoshi no Harae|ja|年越の祓|zh|年越之祓|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Toshikoshi no Harae|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} }} {{Ritual ceremonies of the Imperial Palace}} '''Ōharae''' (おおはらえ・おおはらい) is one of the major rites of [[:en:Harae|Harae]] in the [[:en:Shinto|Shinto]] tradition of [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Grounded in the traditional Japanese concern for ritual purity, it aims to cleanse the mind and body of defilements (''kegare'') and remove the various sins and errors that give rise to misfortune, so that people may live each day with a pure and tranquil heart.{{Cite book|language=ja|title=神道いろは―神社とまつりの基礎知識―|date=2007-01-25|publisher=神社新報社|page=116|editor={{ill|Association of Shinto Shrines|de|Jinja-honchō|ja|神社本庁教学研究所|zh|神社本庁教学研究所|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Association of Shinto Shrines|qq=|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}}}} While purification rites (''harae'') are performed routinely at the {{ill|Imperial Court|de|Japanischer Kaiserhof|ja|宮中|zh|日本皇宮|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Imperial Court|qq=}} and in [[:en:Shinto shrine|Shinto shrine]], the twice-yearly ceremonies held for the benefit of all under heaven are distinguished by the name '''Ō-harae''' (“great purification”).''Sekai Daihyakka-jiten'' 2nd ed., s.v. "Ōharae". By long custom the rite is observed on the last day of the Sixth and Twelfth Months—that is, 30 June and 31 December in the modern calendar. In former times it was also conducted ad hoc, for example before and after the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]] (the first ''Niiname-sai'' after an [[:en:Emperor of Japan|Emperor of Japan]]’s accession), in response to unprecedented epidemics or disasters, or to purify candidates for the offices of [[:en:Saikū|Saigū]] and [[:en:Saiin (priestess)|Saiin]]. The ceremony is also called the "Purification of the [[:en:Nakatomi clan|Nakatomi clan]]" ('''Nakatomi-no-Harae'''). == Overview == The earliest textual attestation appears in the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], in the section on [[:en:Emperor Chūai|Emperor Chūai]]: {{quote|Take also the great offerings (''Ō-nusa'') of the land and perform a '''great purification''', removing the sins of raw-hide flaying, reverse flaying, dam-filling, dung-gate, incest, bestiality with horse, ox, fowl, and dog…|Adapted from the [[:en:Kojiki|Kojiki]], Chūai no Maki}} These offences are collectively known as [[:en:Tsumi|Heavenly sins and earthly sins]]. Because ordinary sins (''tsumi'') and ritual defilements (''kegare'') could not be removed by the short everyday formulas (''harae-kotoba''), the lengthy '''Ō-harae Norito''' was proclaimed to cleanse them. The prayer lists the heavenly sins, which largely concern violations of agricultural taboos, before the earthly sins, implying that in ancient times the former were seen as the graver threat to communal order. Originally the texts for the Sixth- and Twelfth-Month rites differed, but the [[:en:Engishiki|Engishiki]] notes "The Twelfth-Month rite shall follow the precedent of the Sixth," so only the Sixth-Month version survives. While today the norito is recited to the kami, the version in the ''Engishiki'' makes clear that the officiant first calls upon the assembled participants to listen, they respond "Ō" (''isshō''), and only then follows the mythic preamble, enumeration of sins, and description of how the {{ill|Haraedo no Kami|de|Haraedo-no-kami|ja|祓戸大神|zh|祓戶大神|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Haraedo no Kami|qq=}} carry them away. Thus Ō-harae not only "resets" calamities that have already occurred and prays for the tranquillity of the realm, it also functioned as a public proclamation of the taboos imposed by the ruling authority.''Sekai Daihyakka-jiten'', 2nd ed., s.v. "Kodai-hō" (ancient law). In 1914 (Taishō 3) the Ministry of Home Affairs replaced the original norito—in which the heavenly and earthly sins contain discriminatory language toward the disabled and other groups—with a truncated text known as the '''Nakatomi Saibun'''.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www2.kokugakuin.ac.jp/kaihatsu/oharai/theme_b.html|title=中臣祓の実践と注釈|publisher=國學院大學 伝統文化リサーチセンター|access-date=2025-04-24}} The modern ritual uses a slightly revised form of this prayer. == Court observances == [[File:Ceremony of the Enthronement of Emperor Shōwa in Shishinden Hall 4.jpg|thumb|right|The enthronement of Emperor Shōwa. Before the ''Ōmikuma-kujin-no-gi'' of the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]], the emperor performs ablutions and the Ō-harae.]] {{See also|Kaijo (ceremony)}} Under the [[:en:Taihō Code|Taihō Code]] of 701, Ō-harae became part of the formal court calendar, with detailed procedures later recorded in the ''Engishiki''. Documents such as ''Gishiki'', ''Hokuzanshō'', and ''E-ke Shidai'' describe the early ceremonies, and the ''Nihon Shoki'' records that in 676 (Tenmu 5) a grand purification ('''Ō-kaijo''') was held in which provincial governors presented horses, cloth, and hemp. The ''Yōrō Code'' prescribes that on the last days of the Sixth and Twelfth Months the Nakatomi present purge-hemp, the court scribes (''Fubito-be'') offer purge-sabres, and at the purification ground—usually before the [[:en:Suzakumon|Suzaku Gate]]—the Nakatomi proclaim the Ō-harae norito to the gathered officials while the diviners (''Urabe'') perform the rites. The ceremony lapsed after the [[:en:Ōnin War|Ōnin War]] devastated Kyoto. In 1871 (Meiji 4) Emperor Meiji revived the rite at the {{ill|Kashiko-dono|de|Kashiko-dono|ja|賢所|1=Kashiko-dokoro|2=ja|3=賢所|4=fr|5=Kashiko-dokoro|zh|賢所|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashiko-dono|13=User:Immanuelle/Kashiko-dokoro|qq=}} of the [[:en:Three Palace Sanctuaries|Three Palace Sanctuaries]], and the following year a proclamation ordered its restoration nationwide.''Nen-chū Gyōji Jiten'' (Encyclopedia of Annual Rites), Tokyo-dō Shuppan, 1958, p. 121. Since the adoption of the Western calendar in 1873, the court has observed the rite on 30 June and 31 December. The ceremony was duly performed for the [[:en:Daijosai|Daijō-sai]] in the Taishō, Shōwa, and Heisei eras. In 2014 the [[:en:Imperial Household Agency|Imperial Household Agency]], noting the decline in adult male princes, announced that henceforth adult female royals could also attend the rite.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://www.sankei.com/article/20140610- 000 |title=6月・12月「大祓の儀」ご参列　女性皇族にも拡大|publisher=産経ニュース|date=2014-06-10|access-date=2025-04-24}} == Popular observance == [[File:Ohyamato-jinja02s3200.jpg|thumb|right|A chinowa ring at [[:en:Ōyamato Shrine|Ōyamato Shrine]]]] Among the populace, the ceremonies have long been observed as rites of expiation: the Sixth-Month rite is commonly called '''Nagoshi-no-Harae''' (“summer purification”) and the Twelfth-Month rite '''Toshikoshi-no-Harae''' (“year-end purification”). Local variations include holding the ritual one month later (31 July) to match the lunar calendar. === Nagoshi-no-Harae === The ''Shūi Wakashū'' already contains an anonymous poem: "On Nagoshi-no-Harae in the Month of Waterless Moon, those who purify themselves are said to prolong their lives a thousand years." In an age when laundering clothes daily and abundant clean water were luxuries, replacing garments before the humid summer months was thought to ward off disease. The date also marks the end of the rainy season in most regions, a time to steel oneself for the coming heat and drought. After the rite fell into abeyance at court, it survived only in a few shrines and, from 1691 (Genroku 4), in limited form under names such as "Nagoshi Shinji".[[:en:Matsunoo Taisha|Matsuo Shrine]] official site, "Ōharae-shiki". The 1871 proclamation restoring Ō-harae nationwide also discouraged alternative names, but in the post-war era terms like "Nagoshi Shinji" have again come into use. ==== Passing through the Chinowa ==== At many shrines the highlight of Nagoshi-no-Harae is passing through a great ring of cogon grass (''chinowa''). A hoop several metres in diameter is set up in the approach, often within a rope-enclosed sacred space. Parishioners walk through it left, right, and left again in a figure-eight, thereby shedding the ailments and defilements of the past six months. In bygone days people wore small rings of grass on the body. This custom derives from the legend of [[:en:Somin Shōrai|Somin Shōrai]] in the [[:en:Bingo (American version)|Bingo Province]] fragment: the deity Mutō no Kami (identified with [[:en:Susanoo-no-Mikoto|Susanoo-no-Mikoto]]) instructed Somin-shōrai to wear a ring of grass to escape a plague. Some shrines dismantle the ring afterwards and allow worshippers to take pieces home, but a 2011 article in the ''Kyoto Shimbun'' cautioned that the grass has absorbed the participants’ defilements and should not be removed.''Kyoto Shimbun'', 24 June 2011, p. 24. Variants include the triple ring of cedar, pine, and sakaki at [[:en:Ōmiwa Shrine|Ōmiwa Shrine]] in Nara, and the "U-shaped" chinowa of [[:en:Izumo-taisha|Izumo Taisha]], which worshippers leap over while discarding a bundle of grass from their shoulders.''Izumo Taishakyō Bukkyōshi Yōsei Kōshūkai'', Izumo Taishakyō Headquarters, 1989, p. 331. The custom has even been extended to pets, especially dogs.Aloha Street, "Chinowa and Pet Purification at Hawaii Kotohira Shrine & Hawai‘i Dazaifu Tenmangū", 2019. {{Commonscat|Chinowa|茅の輪}} === Use of ''Hitogata'' Paper Figures === Another practice is to breathe upon or rub a small human-shaped paper doll (''hitogata'') to transfer one’s impurities, then cast it into a river or the sea. Such dolls, and later {{ill|Tanzaku|de|Tanzaku|ja|短冊|zh|短冊|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Tanzaku|qq=}} inscribed at the [[:en:Qixi Festival|Tanabata]] festival, were occasionally burnt, a custom influenced by [[:en:Sagichō Fire Festival|Dondoyaki]] bonfires and esoteric Buddhist rites. === Food customs === In Kyoto it is customary to eat the confection '''{{ill|Minazuki (sweet)|de|Minazuki (Süßspeise)|ja|水無月 (和菓子)|zh|水無月 (菓子)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Minazuki (sweet)|qq=}}'''—triangular ''u­i­ro­u'' topped with adzuki beans that symbolise ice and repel evil.{{Cite web|language=ja|url=https://ja.kyoto.travel/event/season/june/|title=夏越の祓|publisher=京都市観光協会|access-date=2025-04-24}} Since 2015 a promotional "'''Nagoshi Gohan'''"—a bowl of multigrain rice topped with a round fritter of summer vegetables—has been advocated by the public organisation "MAFF Net" to mark the occasion.''Yomiuri Shimbun'', 26 June 2015. In parts of [[:en:Kōchi Prefecture|Kōchi Prefecture]], the rite is nicknamed "'''Wanuke-sama'''" ("Passing-through-the-Ring"). == Notes == {{Notelist}} == References == {{Reflist|2}} == See also == * {{ill|Setsubiki|de|Setsubiki|ja|節折|1=Yoori|2=ja|3=節折|4=fr|5=Yoori|6=simple|7=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|zh|節折|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Setsubiki|13=User:Immanuelle/Yoori|qq=}} * [[:en:Garland|Garland]] == External links == * {{Kotobank|大祓}} {{translated page|ja|大祓|version=103420033|comment=Imported full ja history}} {{draft categories| {{draft categories| [[Category:Festivals in Japan]] [[Category:Exorcism in Shinto]] [[Category:Ritual purification]] [[Category:Shinto_festivals]] [[Category:Onmyōdō]] [[Category:Shinbutsu_shūgō]] [[Category:Lunisolar June]] [[Category:日本の旧暦]] [[Category:Lunisolar December]] [[Category:日本の旧暦]] [[Category:Completion tier 1]] }} [[ja:大祓]] [[sn:Ōharae-shiki]] [[sn:大祓]] [[en:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ar:Ōharae-shiki]] [[de:Ooharae]] [[Category:December]] [[Category:June]] [[Category:Buddhist holidays]] [[Category:夏の季語]] [[Category:Annual events in Japan]] [[Category:Japanese Imperial Rituals]] [[Category:Shinbutsu shūgō]] [[Category:Shinto festivals]] [[Category:除災]] [[Category:雑節]] {{Commons category|Ōharae}} [[fr:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ko:오하라에]] {{Commons category|Ōharae}} [[fr:Ōharae-shiki]] [[ko:오하라에]] [[Category:translated pages with valid en interwikis]] [[Category:Japanese Imperial Rituals]] [[Category:qq]][[sn:Ōharae-shiki]][[Category:qq]]
